access: Free. Park Brakkenstein / Landgoed Brakkenstein is a public city park in south Nijmegen (Heijendaal), used for walking and recreation; the star-forest (sterrenbos) layout dates to 18th-century maps. Confirmed as public via nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Brakkenstein and monumenten.nl/monument/522933 (Rijksmonument description), both fetched directly. The 1865 neoclassical villa beside which this tree stands is now an event/restaurant venue (landgoedbrakkesteyn.nl); the surrounding park grounds themselves are ordinary open parkland, not gated.
transport: South Nijmegen, Heijendaal area near Radboud University and Radboud UMC; nearest bus stop not pinned this pass, honest gap.
story:
Nijmegen's own city register and the national monumental tree register agree on almost nothing about this horse chestnut except where it stands. One says it went into the ground around 1830, making it nearly two centuries old. The other says 1920, barely past its first century. Neither figure is a measurement, both are estimates carried on separate paperwork, and eighty years is too wide a gap to average away.

What both records do agree on is the spot: a trunk about two and three quarter metres round, standing by the villa at Landgoed Brakkenstein, a star-shaped eighteenth-century park layout in Heijendaal. The estate's own lanes were planted mostly with beech, except for one western avenue lined in horse chestnuts, which raises the honest possibility that this tree began as part of that planting rather than a lone specimen chosen for the villa's front lawn.

The 1865 neoclassical villa it grows beside now hosts events and dinners rather than a resident family, but the grounds around it stay open the way a city park is open: no gate, no ticket, just a walk through Heijendaal past Radboud University. Two registers, two ages, one honest tree, and a question nobody has settled: was it planted for the house, or was it already there?
verify_notes: Two independent official registers place a horse chestnut within 1.2m of each other at this exact spot, which clears the two-source bar on existence, species and location: LRMB (Bomenstichting, national) and the Gemeente Nijmegen municipal tree-management dataset (BOR_Groen, CC-BY, separate provenance from LRMB, confirmed reachable per data/fetch-blocklist.json's 2026-08-26 update). Species agrees exactly (Aesculus hippocastanum). AGE CONFLICTS SHARPLY and is not resolved: LRMB's planted_band 1830-1840 implies roughly 186-196 years old (2026); the municipal record's plantjaar 1920 implies roughly 106 years old, a 80-90 year gap. Neither figure is corroborated by a third source. Do not silently pick one; state the disagreement on the page if an age is mentioned at all, or omit it. GIRTH: municipal record gives stamdiameter class '75 tot 100 cm' (a diameter, not circumference); midpoint 87.5cm converted via circumference=pi*diameter gives ~275cm girth, recorded as girth_cm but this is a derived conversion from a binned diameter class, not a direct tape measurement, flag that provenance if girth is quoted. CONTEXT WORTH THE STORY: nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Brakkenstein (fetched directly) describes the park's star-forest lanes as 'largely planted with beech trees, except for the most western lane where horse chestnuts stand and the section of the diagonal behind the villa where linden trees are planted' -- this raises a real possibility that this chestnut is part of that western chestnut-lined lane rather than a fully standalone specimen 'by the villa' as the register's place-name implies; a future pass or a photo/aerial check should confirm whether it stands free of that lane structure before the story calls it a lone specimen. The register's own place field, 'bij het landhuis', and its separate, distinct status from the previously-BLOCKED avenue entry (register nr 1681243, 'Beukenlaan nabij restaurant', ~230m away) is the reason it was treated as an individually designated point rather than folded into the avenue exclusion. Villa built 1865 (neoclassical, replacing an older manor); estate has a documented 1970s botanical garden layer added by the Catholic University. No news or death report found for this specific tree (the sweet-chestnut/tamme kastanje death report at 'de Drie Huizen' elsewhere on the estate, found by an earlier pass, is a different tree of a different species and does not apply here).

story:
Fifteen metres from that horse chestnut stands a beech with a trunk over four metres round, thick enough that the city's own register lists a diameter class normally reserved for trees decades older than the planting date on file. That mismatch is the interesting part: the municipal record says 1880, about 146 years ago, while the national monumental tree register puts it at 1830 to 1840, closer to 190. A trunk this size fits the older number better, though nobody has resolved the disagreement and neither figure is a measurement rather than an estimate.

It stands at Landgoed Brakkenstein, the eighteenth-century star-forest park in Heijendaal, beside the 1865 villa that gives both this tree and its chestnut neighbour their address. The park's own lanes were mostly planted in beech, so this could be an individual designation rather than a lane tree: its diameter class runs well above the beeches recorded along the avenue nearby, which is one reason it earned its own spot on the register rather than being folded into the avenue as a whole.

Free to see, in an ordinary public park near Radboud University, no gate and no ticket. Two records, two ages, and a trunk that seems to be arguing for the older one.
verify_notes: Same pattern and same two-source match quality as nij_019 immediately above, ~15m away: LRMB and the Gemeente Nijmegen BOR_Groen dataset independently place a beech within 2.9m of each other, both flag it monumentaal, species agrees exactly (Fagus sylvatica). AGE CONFLICTS, smaller gap than the chestnut but still real: LRMB planted_band 1830-1840 implies roughly 186-196 years; municipal plantjaar 1880 implies roughly 146 years, a 40-50 year gap. Do not pick a winner silently. One point worth passing to the writer: the municipal stamdiameter class here is 125-150cm, genuinely large for a beech (girth ~432cm derived via circumference=pi*diameter from the 137.5cm midpoint, same caveat as nij_019 that this is a converted diameter class, not a tape measurement), which fits an older tree better than the 146-year municipal planting figure does; this is reasoning, not a resolution, and should not be used to silently prefer the LRMB figure. NOT the same register entry as the previously-BLOCKED Beukenlaan avenue tree (register nr 1681243, ~230m away, explicitly on a beech-lined lane 'nabij restaurant'): this entry's place field reads 'bij het landhuis' like the chestnut beside it, distinguishing it from that avenue designation, which is why it was treated as its own point rather than folded into the avenue exclusion. Same western-park-layout caveat as nij_019 applies in principle (the park's lanes are 'largely planted with beech trees' per nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Brakkenstein, fetched directly) though this specimen's unusually large stated diameter (125-150cm, well above the ~50-100cm range recorded for the actual lane-planted Tilia avenue trees seen in the same municipal dataset pull) is itself evidence this is a distinguishable individual rather than a run-of-the-lane tree.
